name: Rahab

seo.title: Rahab of Jericho: her life, the scarlet cord and her faith
seo.description: Rahab in plain words: the woman of Jericho who hid Joshua's spies, the scarlet cord, her place in the family line of Jesus, and the myths.

band.lede: A woman of Jericho who hid Joshua's spies and trusted their God. When the city fell, she and her family were spared, and Matthew counts her among the ancestors of Jesus.

who: Rahab was a prostitute in Jericho, and her house was built into the city wall. She hid two of Joshua's spies, told them the LORD had given Israel the land, and let them down by a rope. She tied a scarlet cord in her window, and when Jericho fell, her whole family was spared.

tidbits.text: The Hebrew word for her scarlet **cord** is **tiqvah**. Everywhere else in the Bible, the same word means **hope**.

cite.text: Joshua 2:18, 21; Strong's Hebrew 8615, at Bible Hub

tidbits.text: Hebrews 11 names only two women among its heroes of faith: **Sarah** and **Rahab**. And when James wants two examples of faith shown in deeds, he picks **Abraham** and **Rahab**.
Dante puts her in heaven. In his *Paradiso* she shines in the heaven of Venus, the first soul that Christ’s triumph brought there: “First of Christ’s triumph was she taken up.”

cite.text: Dante, *Paradiso*, canto 9, tr. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

facts.label: In the Bible
facts.text: **Joshua** 2 and 6. The New Testament names her three times: in **Matthew** 1, **Hebrews** 11 and **James** 2.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: **Jericho**, near the fords of the Jordan. Her house was built into the **city wall**, with a window on the outside.

facts.label: Her people
facts.text: A **Canaanite** of Jericho, not an Israelite. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus saw in her the Gentiles coming to Christ.

facts.label: Her name
facts.text: From the Hebrew for **broad** or **wide**. It is spelled differently from the **Rahab** of the Psalms, a poetic name for Egypt.

facts.label: Her trade
facts.text: A **prostitute**, as the book of Joshua says, and Hebrews and James after it. Josephus, a Jewish historian of the first century, calls her house an **inn**.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: Her father, mother, brothers and sisters, all spared with her. Matthew names the father of her son **Boaz**: **Salmon**, of the tribe of Judah.

facts.label: When
facts.text: As Israel crossed the **Jordan** under **Joshua**, after forty years in the wilderness.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Rahab the harlot**, in older English Bibles and in the Fathers. **Raab**, in the Greek of Hebrews and James.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Letting the spies down from her window, or with the **scarlet cord**, as at the top of this page.

quotes.q: By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient.
quotes.who: The letter to the Hebrews, in its roll call of the faithful

quotes.q: In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route?
quotes.who: James, straight after Abraham, on faith shown in deeds

quotes.q: He gave her certain lands immediately, and had her in great esteem ever afterwards.
quotes.who: Josephus, the Jewish historian, writing about 93, on what Joshua did for her after Jericho fell

cite.text: Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 5, chapter 1

quotes.q: And thus they made it manifest that redemption should flow through the blood of the Lord to all them that believe and hope in God. Ye see, beloved, that there was not only faith, but prophecy, in this woman.
quotes.who: Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth about 97, on the scarlet cord. Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and Ambrose read it the same way.

quotes.q: The typical Jesus saved Rahab the harlot when she believed: and the true Jesus says, Behold, the publicans and the harlots go before you into the kingdom of God.
quotes.who: Cyril of Jerusalem, teaching those about to be baptised, about 350. In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are one name, so Joshua is “the typical Jesus”: the type, or foreshadowing, of Christ.

quotes.q: For this end he hath mentioned Ruth also and Rahab, the one an alien, the other an harlot, that thou mayest learn that He came to do away with all our ills. For He hath come as a Physician, not as a Judge.
quotes.who: John Chrysostom, on why Matthew names her among the ancestors of Jesus

moments.title: Two spies at her door
moments.text: Joshua “secretly sent two spies from Shittim” to look over the land, especially Jericho. “So they went and entered the house of a prostitute named Rahab and stayed there.” Word reached the king of Jericho, and he sent to her: “Bring out the men who came to you”. She had already hidden them on her roof, among the stalks of flax she had laid out there. Yes, she said, the men had come, but they had left at dusk, when the gate was about to close. “Pursue them quickly, and you may catch them!” The king's men set off along the road to the fords of the Jordan, and the gate was shut behind them.

moments.title: “Your God is God”
moments.text: Before the spies lay down, Rahab went up to them on the roof. “I know that the LORD has given you this land”, she said. Jericho had heard how the LORD dried up the Red Sea, and what Israel had done to Sihon and Og, two kings across the Jordan. “When we heard this, our hearts melted”. Then she made her confession, given below in her own words. She asked them to swear by the LORD to spare her father and mother, her brothers and sisters. “Our lives for your lives!” the men agreed.

moments.title: The scarlet cord
moments.text: Her house was built into the city wall, so she let them down by a rope through the window. “Go to the hill country,” she told them, and hide there three days. The men gave her a sign. When Israel came, she must tie “this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down”, and bring her whole family inside. Anyone who went out into the street would be on his own. “Let it be as you say,” she replied. When they had gone, she tied the scarlet cord in the window. The spies hid three days in the hills, then went back to Joshua: “The LORD has surely delivered the entire land into our hands”.

moments.title: The wall falls
moments.text: Jericho was shut tight. For six days Israel marched around the city once a day, with seven priests blowing rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day they went around seven times. Before the shout, Joshua gave an order: “Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent.” The horns sounded, the people shouted, “and the wall collapsed.” Joshua sent the two spies into her house to bring her out, “just as you promised her.” They brought out her whole family and settled them outside the camp. The rest of the city was destroyed and burned.

moments.title: In the line of David
moments.text: Joshua spared her, with her father's household, “because she hid the men Joshua had sent to spy out Jericho.” The book of Joshua ends her story simply: “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day.” Matthew adds what came next. She became the mother of Boaz, by a man of Judah named Salmon. Boaz married Ruth, and their grandson Jesse was the father of King David. So Matthew writes her into the family line of Jesus: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab”.

words.note: Rahab wrote nothing. These are her words as the book of Joshua records them. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.kicker: On her roof, to the spies
feature.q: When we heard this, our hearts melted and everyone’s courage failed because of you, for the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below.
feature.ctx: The king's men had gone off toward the Jordan. She went up to the two spies hidden under her flax, and told them what Jericho had heard.

quotes.q: Yes, the men did come to me, but I did not know where they had come from. At dusk, when the gate was about to close, the men went out, and I do not know which way they went. Pursue them quickly, and you may catch them!
quotes.who: To the king's men, with the spies hidden on her roof.

quotes.q: I know that the LORD has given you this land and that the fear of you has fallen on us, so that all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of you.
quotes.who: Her first words to the spies.

quotes.q: For we have heard how the LORD dried up the waters of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt.
quotes.who: What Jericho had heard, forty years on.

quotes.q: Now therefore, please swear to me by the LORD that you will indeed show kindness to my family, because I showed kindness to you.
quotes.who: Asking the spies for an oath, for her father and mother, her brothers and sisters.

quotes.q: Go to the hill country, so that your pursuers will not find you. Hide yourselves there for three days until they have returned; then go on your way.

extras.title: Was she right to lie?
extras.lede: To save the spies, she told the king's men they had already gone. Christians have argued about that lie ever since. Here each side speaks for itself.

items.title: What the Bible praises
items.text: Joshua spared her “because she hid the spies we sent.” Hebrews praises her faith: she “welcomed the spies in peace.” James praises her deeds: she “welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route.” None of them mentions what she told the king's men.

items.title: Augustine: the kindness, not the lie
items.text: Augustine held that a Christian may never lie, even to save a life. God rewarded Rahab, he says, “not because they lied, but because they were merciful to God's people.” More could not yet be asked of her, for she did not yet belong to God's people. For hiding the spies, for her faith and for her good counsel, “let her be praised”. But her lie was forgiven, not held up to copy.
items.quote: That therefore which was rewarded in them was, not their deceit, but their benevolence; benignity of mind, not iniquity of lying.

items.title: Cassian: a medicine for deadly danger
items.text: In John Cassian's *Conferences*, the Egyptian monk Abba Joseph takes the other side. A lie, he says, is like hellebore, a poisonous plant used as medicine: deadly to the healthy, a remedy when death is near. Had Rahab told the truth, she and her house would have died with the city. She would never have been “inserted in the progenitors of our Lord's nativity”. Even so, he warns:
items.quote: When then any grave danger hangs on confession of the truth, then we must take to lying as a refuge, yet in such a way as to be for our salvation troubled by the guilt of a humbled conscience.

myths.claim: Rahab was an innkeeper, not a prostitute.
myths.truth: The Bible calls her a prostitute. The book of Joshua does, and so do Hebrews and James. The gentler reading is old, though. Josephus, writing in the first century, has the spies lodge in “the inn kept by Rahab”. An Aramaic paraphrase of Joshua made her an innkeeper, the *Jewish Encyclopedia* notes, and the medieval Jewish scholar Rashi followed it. The Talmud itself takes her for a harlot.

cite.text: Joshua 2:1; Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25; Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 5, chapter 1; *Jewish Encyclopedia*, “Rahab”

myths.claim: The Rahab of the Psalms is Rahab of Jericho.
myths.truth: They are two different words. In Hebrew they are spelled with different letters, and hers means broad. The other Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt, and for a monster of the sea. Isaiah calls Egypt “Rahab Who Sits Still”, and Psalm 89 says to God, “You crushed Rahab like a carcass.” Some Fathers still heard Psalm 87 as about her: “I will mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me.” Cyril of Jerusalem did, and so did Ambrose. The 1894 English edition of Cyril adds a note: the psalm “has nothing to do with Rahab the harlot.”

cite.text: Isaiah 30:7; Psalm 87:4; 89:10; Strong's Hebrew 7343 and 7294; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lectures*, Lecture 2, with its note

myths.truth: Not in the Bible. The book of Joshua says only that she lived among the Israelites, and Matthew names Salmon as the father of her son Boaz. The marriage to Joshua is a Jewish tradition, found in the Talmud. It adds that eight prophets who were also priests came from her, Jeremiah among them, and the prophetess Huldah.

cite.text: Joshua 6:25; Matthew 1:5; *Jewish Encyclopedia*, “Rahab”, on the Talmud, tractate Megillah

circle.name: Ruth
circle.text: Her daughter-in-law, by Matthew's reckoning: Ruth married her son Boaz. Another woman from outside Israel who came to trust Israel's God.

circle.name: David
circle.text: Her great-great-grandson, by Matthew's family line: Boaz, Obed, Jesse, then “David the king”.

circle.name: Joshua
circle.text: Moses' successor. He sent the two spies from Shittim, and when Jericho fell he sent them to bring her out, with all her family.

circle.name: The two spies
circle.text: Joshua's men, never named. She hid them under her flax and let them down from her window. They swore to spare her house, and kept their word.

circle.name: The king of Jericho
circle.text: He heard that spies had come and sent to her house for them. She sent his men off down the road to the Jordan.

circle.name: Salmon
circle.text: The father of her son, in Matthew's line. The book of Ruth names him as the father of Boaz, but only Matthew names Rahab as the mother.

circle.name: Boaz
circle.text: Her son. He was the kind landowner of Bethlehem who married Ruth, and the great-grandfather of David.

saint.big: The New Testament counts her among the faithful, and the Fathers praised her faith. But she has no feast day of her own. East and West remember her with the ancestors of Christ just before Christmas, when her name is read out in the Gospel.

churches.note: With Christ's ancestors, the Sunday before Christmas
Church of England and Episcopal Church

paras: On the last Sunday before Christmas, the Orthodox remember the forefathers of Christ. The Gospel that day is Matthew's family line of Jesus, with its line “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab”.
Rome's book of martyrs keeps 24 December for all the holy forefathers of Jesus Christ. That evening, at the vigil Mass of Christmas, the Gospel is the same family line.
